17.text: That is, by death the cruelty of the tyrants has ceased.

18.text: All they who sustain any kind of calamity and misery in this world: which he speaks after the judgment of the flesh.

2.text: Seeing your impatience.

3.text: You have comforted others in their afflictions but you cannot now comfort yourself.

6.text: He concludes that Job was a hypocrite and had no true fear or trust in God.

7.text: He concludes that Job was reproved seeing that God handles him so extremely, which is the argument that the carnal men make against the children of God.

8.text: They who do evil cannot but receive evil.

9.text: He shows that God needs no great preparation to destroy his enemies: for he can do it with the blast of his mouth.

10.text: Though men according to their office do not punish tyrants

20.text: They see death continually before their eyes and daily approaching them.

1.text: He wills Job to consider the example of all who have lived or live godly, whether any of them are like him in raging against God as he does.

2.text: Murmuring against God in afflictions increases the pain, and uttered man’s folly.

3.text: That is, the sinner that does not have the fear of God.
I was not moved by his prosperity but knew that God had cursed him and his.

4.text: Though God sometimes allows the father’s to pass in this world, yet his judgments will light on their wicked children.
By public judgment they will be condemned and no one will pity them.

5.text: Though there are only two or three ears left in the hedges, yet these will be taken from him.

6.text: That is, the earth is not the cause of barrenness and man’s misery, but his own sin.

7.text: Which declares that sin is always in our corrupt nature: for before sin it was not subject to pain and affliction.

8.text: If I suffered as you do, I would seek God.

9.text: He counsels Job to humble himself to God to whom all creatures are subject and whose works declare that man is inexcusable unless he glorifies God in all his works.

14.text: In things plain and evident they show themselves fools instead of wise men.

15.text: That is, he who humbles himself before God.

16.text: If the wicked are compelled by God’s works to shut their mouths, how much more they who profess God.

22.text: While the wicked lament in their troubles, you will have occasion to rejoice.

23.text: When we are in God’s favour, all creatures will serve us.

24.text: God will so bless you that you will have opportunity to rejoice in all things, and not be offended.

26.text: Though the children of God have not always carried out this promise, yet God recompenses it otherwise to their advantage.

27.text: We have learned these points by experience, that God does not punish the innocent, that man cannot compare in justice with him, that the hypocrites will not prosper for long, and that the affliction which man sustains comes for his own sin.

3.text: My grief is so great that I lack words to express it.

4.text: Which declares that he was not only afflicted in body, but wounded in conscience, which is the greatest battle that the faithful can have.

5.text: Do you think that I cry without cause, seeing the brute beasts do not complain when they have what they want.

6.text: Can a man’s taste delight in that, which has no savour? meaning that no one takes pleasure in affliction seeing they cannot do away with things that are unsavoury to the mouth.

8.text: In this he sins double, both in wishing through impatience to die, and also in desiring of God a thing which was not agreeable to his will.

10.text: That is, let me die at once before I come to distrust God’s promise through my impatience.

11.text: He fears lest he should be brought to inconveniences, if his sorrows should continue.

13.text: Have I not sought to help myself as much as was possible?

15.text: He compares friends who do not comfort us in our misery to a brook which in summer when we need water is dry, in winter is hard frozen and in the time of rain when we have no need overflows with water.

19.text: They who pass by it to go into the hot countries of Arabia, think to find water there to quench their thirst but they are deceived.

21.text: That is, like this brook which deceives them who think to have water there in their need, as I looked for consolation from you.

22.text: He touches the worldlings who for need will give part of their goods, and much more these men, who would not give him comfortable words.

24.text: Show me where I have erred, and I will confess my sin.

25.text: He who has a good conscience does not shrink at the sharp words or reasonings of others, unless they are able to persuade him by reason.

26.text: Do you object to my words because I would be thought to speak foolishly, and am now in misery?

1.text: Has not a hired servant some rest and ease? Then in this my continual torment I am worse than a hireling.

3.text: My sorrow has continued from month to month, and I have looked for hope in vain.

5.text: This signifies that his disease was rare and most horrible.

6.text: Thus he speaks in respect for the brevity of man’s life, which passes without hope of returning: in consideration of which he desires God to have compassion on him.

9.text: If you behold me in your anger I will not be able to stand in your presence.
Shall no more enjoy this mortal life.

11.text: Seeing I can by no other means comfort myself I will declare my grief in words, and thus he speaks as one overcome with grief of mind.

12.text: Am I not a poor wretch? Why do you need to lay so much pain on me?

14.text: So that I can have no rest, night or day.

15.text: He speaks as one overcome with sorrow, and not of judgment, or of the examination of his faith.

17.text: Seeing that man of himself is so vile, why do you give him that honour to contend against him? Job uses all kinds of persuasion with God, that he might stay his hand.

21.text: That is, I will be dead.

2.text: He declares that their words which would diminish anything from the justice of God, are but as a puff of wind that vanishes away.

5.text: That is, if you turn while God calls you to repentance.

8.text: He wills Job to examine all antiquity and he will find it true which he here says.

9.text: Meaning, that it is not enough to have the experience of ourselves, but to be confirmed by the examples of those who went before us.

11.text: As a rush cannot grow without moisture, so the hypocrite because he does not have faith which is watered with God’s Spirit.

14.text: Which is today and tomorrow swept away.

21.text: If you are godly, he will give you opportunity to rejoice and if not your affliction will increase.

2.text: Job here answers Eliphaz and Bildad’s oration, touching the justice of God, and his innocency, confessing God to be infinite in justice and man to be nothing in respect.

3.text: Of a thousand things, which God could lay to his charge, man cannot answer him one.

6.text: He declares the infirmity of man, by the mighty and incomprehensible power that is in God, showing what he could do if he would set forth his power.

9.text: These are the names of certain stars by which he means that all stars both known and unknown are at his appointment.

12.text: He shows that when God executes his power, he does it justly, as no one can control him.

13.text: God will not be appeased for anything that man can say for himself for his justification.
That is, all the reasons that men can lay to approve their cause.

14.text: How should I be able to answer him by eloquence? By which he notes his friends, who although they were eloquent in talk, did not believe in their hearts, that which they spoke.

15.text: Meaning, in his own opinion, signifying that man will sometimes flatter himself to be righteous which before God is an abomination.

16.text: While I am in pain I cannot break forth into many inconveniences although I still know that God is just.

17.text: I am not able to feel my sins so great, as I feel the weight of his plagues; and this he speaks to condemn his dullness and to justify God.

19.text: After he has accused his own weakness, he continues to justify God and his power.

22.text: If God punishes according to his justice, he will destroy them who are counted perfect as well as them that are wicked.

23.text: That is, the wicked.

24.text: That they cannot see to do justice.
That can show the contrary?

27.text: I think not to fall into these afflictions, but my sorrows bring me to these manifold infirmities, and my conscience condemns me.

29.text: Why does God not destroy me at once? thus he speaks according to the infirmity of the flesh.

30.text: Though I seem pure in my own eyes, yet all is but corruption before God.

31.text: Whatever I would use to cover my filthiness with, it would disclose me even more.

33.text: Who might make an accord between God and me, speaking of impatience, and yet confessing God to be just in punishing him.

35.text: Signifying that God’s judgments keep him in awe.

1.text: I am more like a dead man, than to one that lives.
I will make an ample declaration of my torments, accusing myself and not God.

2.text: He would not that God would proceed against him by his secret justice, but by the ordinary means that he punishes others.

3.text: Is it agreeable to your justice to do me wrong?
Will you be without compassions?
Will you gratify the wicked and condemn me?

4.text: Do you do this of ignorance.

5.text: Are you inconstant and changeable as the times, today a friend, tomorrow an enemy?

7.text: By affliction you keep me as in a prison, and restrain me from doing evil, neither can any set me free.

9.text: As brittle as a pot of clay.

13.text: Though I am not fully able to comprehend these things, yet I must confess that it is so.

15.text: I will always walk in fear and humility, knowing that no one is just before you.

17.text: That is, diversity of diseases and in great abundance; showing that God has infinite means to punish man.

20.text: He wishes that God would leave off his affliction, considering his great misery and the shortness of his life.

21.text: He speaks this in the person of a sinner, that is overcome with passions and with the feeling of God’s judgments and therefore cannot apprehend in that state the mercies of God, and the comfort of the resurrection.

22.text: No distinction between light and darkness but where there is very darkness itself.

12.text: That is, without understanding, so that whatever gifts he has afterward come from God, and not from nature.

14.text: Renounce your own evil works and see that they do not offend God, over whom you have charge.

2.text: Because you do not feel what you speak, you think the whole stands in words, and so flatter yourselves as though no one else knew anything, or could know except you.

Who being a mocker and a wicked man, thinks that no man is in God’s favour but he, because he has all things that he desires.

5.text: As the rich do not esteem a light or torch that goes out, so he despised he that falls from prosperity to adversity.

7.text: He declares to them that disputed against him, that their wisdom is common to all, and such as the very brute beasts teach daily.

18.text: He takes wisdom from them.
He abates the humour of princes, and brings them into the subjection of others.

20.text: He causes their words to have no credit, which is when he will punish sin.

23.text: In this discourse of God’s wonderful works, Job shows that whatever is done in this world both in the order and change of things, is by God’s will and appointment, in which he declares that he thinks well of God, and is able to set forth his power in words as they that reasoned against him were.

3.text: For although he knew that God was just, which was revealed in his ordinary working and another in his secret counsel, yet he uttered his affection to God, because he was not able to understand the reason he punished him.

4.text: You do not well apply your medicine to the disease.

16.text: By which he declares that he is not a hypocrite as they charged him.

18.text: That is, cleared and not cut off for my sins, as you think.

21.text: He shows what these two things are.

That is, relieve my pain and take me to mercy.

2.text: That is, vain words, and without consolation?

22.text: Out of that misery to which he once fell.

23.text: God not only impoverishes the wicked often, but even in their prosperity he punishes them with a greediness to gain even more: which is as a beggary.

24.text: He shows the weapons God uses against the wicked, who lift up themselves against him, that is, terror of conscience and outward afflictions.

27.text: That is, he was so puffed up with prosperity and abundance for all things, that he forgave God: noting that Job in his happiness did not have the true fear of God.

29.text: Meaning, that his sumptuous buildings would never come to perfection.

31.text: He stands in his own conceit, that he will give no place to good counsel, therefore his own pride will bring him to destruction.

34.text: Who were built or maintained by bribery.

35.text: Therefore all their vain devises will turn to their own destruction.

5.text: If this were in my power, yet I would comfort you and not do as you do to me.

7.text: Meaning, God.

8.text: In token of sorrow and grief.

And answers for you?

Whom you take to be only beasts, as in Job 12:7 .

1.text: The prophet shows that even though God permits the wicked tyrants to oppress his Church for a time, yet eventually he will take revenge on them.

2.text: No stable firmness to settle my feet.

6.text: Do not let my evil entreaty of the enemy be an opportunity for the faithful to fall from you.

1.text: He prays to God with full assurance of faith, that he will deliver him from his adversaries.

4.text: They were not content to take the Church as prisoner: but sought to utterly destroy it.

5.text: By all secret means.
They thought to have subverted your counsel in which the constancy of the Church was established.

8.text: The wickedness of the Ammonites and Moabites is described in that they provoked these other nations to fight against the Israelites.

9.text: By these examples they were confirmed that God would not permit his people to be completely destroyed, Jud 7:21,4:15.

10.text: Trodden under foot as mire.

12.text: That is, Judea: for where his Church is, there he dwells among them.

13.text: Because the reprobate could by no means be amended, he prays that they may utterly be destroyed, be unstable and led by all winds.

16.text: That is, be compelled by your plagues to confess your power.

18.text: Though they do not believe, yet they may prove by experience, that it is in vain to resist against your counsel in establishing your Church.

1.text: David complains that he cannot have access to the Church of God to make profession of his faith, and to profit in religion.

2.text: For only the priests could enter the sanctuary and the rest of the people into the courts.

3.text: So that the poor birds have more freedom than I.

5.text: Who trusts nothing in himself but in you only, and learns from you to rule his life.

6.text: So that the poor birds have more freedom than I.

7.text: They are never weary but increase in strength and courage till they come to God’s house.

9.text: That is, for Christ’s sake, whose figure I represent.

10.text: He would rather live one day in God’s Church than a thousand in the world.

11.text: But will from time to time increase his blessings toward his more and more.

1.text: They confess that God’s free mercy was the cause of their deliverance because he loved the land which he had chosen.

2.text: You have buried them that they will not come into judgment.

3.text: Not only in withdrawing your rod, but in forgiving sins, and in touching our hearts to confess them.

5.text: As in times past they had felt God’s mercies, so now being oppressed by the long continuance of evil, they pray to God that according to his nature he would be merciful to them.

7.text: He confesses that our salvation comes only from God’s mercy.

8.text: He will send all prosperity to his Church, when he has sufficiently corrected them, also by his punishments the faithful will learn to beware that they not return the same offences.

11.text: Though for a time God thus exercises them with his rods, yet under the kingdom of Christ they should have peace and joy.

13.text: Justice will then flourish and have free course and passage in every place.

1.text: David, when persecuted by Saul, prayed this way, leaving the same to the Church as a monument, how to seek relief against their miseries.

2.text: I am not an enemy to them, but I pity them even though they are cruel to me.

3.text: Which was a fair token that he believed that God would deliver him.

5.text: He confesses that God is good to all but only merciful to poor sinners.

6.text: By crying and calling continually he shows how we must not be weary, even though God does not immediately grant our request but that we must earnestly and often call on him.

8.text: He condemns all idols as they can do nothing to declare that they are gods.

9.text: This proves that David prayed in the Name of Christ the Messiah of whose kingdom he here prophecies.

11.text: He confesses himself ignorant till God has taught him, and his heart variable and separate from God, till God join it to him, and confirm it in his obedience.

13.text: That is, from most great danger of death: out of which none but the almighty hand of God could deliver him.

14.text: He shows that there can be no moderation or equity where proud tyrants reign, and that the lack of God’s fear is as a privilege to all vice and cruelty.

16.text: He boasts not of his own virtues, but confesses that God of his free goodness has always been merciful to him, and given him power against his enemies, as to one of his own household.

1.text: God chose that place among the hills to establish Jerusalem and his temple.

3.text: Though your glorious estate does not yet appear, wait with patience and God will accomplish his promise.

4.text: That is, Egypt and these other countries will come to the knowledge of God.
It will be said of him who is regenerate and come to the Church, that he is as one who was born in the Church.

5.text: Out of all quarters they will come to the Church, and be counted as citizens.

6.text: When he calls them by his word into the Church, whom he had elected and written in the book.

7.text: The prophet sets his whole affections and comfort in the church.

1.text: That is, to humble. It was the beginning of a song by which tune this psalm was sung.
Though many cry in their sorrows, yet they cry not earnestly to God for remedy as he did whom he confessed to be the author of his salvation.

5.text: For he who is dead is free from all cares and business of this life and thus he says because he was unprofitable for all matters concerning man’s life, and as it were cut off from this world.
That is, from your providence and care, which is meant according to the judgment of the flesh.

7.text: The storms of your wrath have overwhelmed me.

8.text: He attributes the loss and displeasure of his friends to God’s providence by which he partly punishes and partly tries his.
I see no end to my sorrows.

9.text: My eyes and face declare my sorrows.

10.text: He shows that the time is more convenient for God to help when men call to him in their dangers, than to tarry till they are dead, and then raise them up again.

12.text: That is, in the grave, where only the body lies without all sense and remembrance.

15.text: I am always in great dangers and sorrows as though my life would utterly be cut off every moment.

1.text: Though the horrible confusion of things might cause them to despair of God’s favour, yet the manifold examples of his mercies cause them to trust in God though to man’s judgment they saw no reason to.

2.text: As he who surely believed in heart.
As your invisible heaven is not subject to any alteration and change: so shall the truth of your promise be unchangeable.

3.text: The prophet shows what the promise of God was, on which he grounded his faith.

5.text: The angels will praise your power and faithfulness in delivering your Church.

6.text: Meaning, the angels.

7.text: If the angels tremble before God’s majesty and infinite justice, what earthly creature by oppressing the Church dares to set himself against God?

9.text: For as he delivered the Church by the Red sea, and by destroying Rahab, that is, the Egyptians, so will he deliver it, when the dangers are great.

12.text: Tabor is a mountain west from Jerusalem, and Hermon to the East, so the prophet signifies that all parts and places of the world will obey God’s power for the deliverance of his Church.

14.text: For by this he judges the world and shows himself to be a merciful father and faithful protector to his.

15.text: Feeling in their conscience that God is their father.
They will be preserved by your fatherly providence.

17.text: In that they are preserved and continue, they should give the praise and glory to you alone.

18.text: In that our King has power to defend us, it is the gift of God.

19.text: To Samuel and to others, to assure that David was the chosen one.
Whom I have both chosen and given strength to execute his office, as in Psalms 89:21 .

23.text: Though there will always be enemies against God’s kingdom yet he promises to overcome them.

24.text: I will mercifully perform my promise to him despite his infirmities and offences.
His power, glory and estate.

25.text: He will enjoy the land around him.

26.text: His excellent dignity will appear in this, that he will be named the son of God and the firstborn in which he is a figure of Christ.

29.text: Though for the sins of the people the state of the kingdom decayed, yet God reserved still a root till he had accomplished this promise in Christ.

33.text: Though the faithful answer not in all points to their profession, yet God will not break his covenant with them.

34.text: For God in promising has respect to his mercy, and not to man’s power in performing.

37.text: As long as the Sun and Moon endure, they will be witnesses to me of this promise.

39.text: Because of the horrible confusion of things, the prophet complains to God, as though he did not see the performance of his promise and thus discharging his cares on God, he resists doubt and impatience.

By this he means the horrible dissipation and tearing of the kingdom which was under Jeroboam, or else by the Spirit of prophecy Ethan speaks of those great miseries which came to pass soon after at the captivity of Babylon.

45.text: He shows that the kingdom fell before it came to perfection or was ripe.

46.text: The prophet in joining prayer with his complaint, shows that his faith never failed.

47.text: Seeing man’s life is short, and you have created man to bestow your benefits on him, unless you hasten to help, death will prevent you.

50.text: He means that God’s enemies not only slandered him behind his back, but also mocked him to his face and as it were cast their injuries in his bosom.

51.text: So he calls them who persecute the Church.
They laugh at us who patiently wait for the coming of your Christ.

1.text: Thus the Scripture refers to the prophets.
You have been as a house and defence to us in all our troubles and travels now this four hundred years.

2.text: You have chosen us to be your people before the foundations of the world were laid.

3.text: Moses by lamenting the frailty and shortness of man’s life moves God to pity.

4.text: Though man thinks his life is long, which is indeed most short, yet though it were a thousand years, yet in God’s sight it is as nothing, and as the watch that lasts only three hours.

5.text: You take them away suddenly as with a flood.

7.text: You called us by the rods to consider the storms of our life and for our sins you shorten our days.

9.text: Our days are not only short but miserable as our sins daily provoke your wrath.

10.text: Meaning according to the common state of life.

11.text: If man’s life for the shortness of it is miserable, it is even more so if your wrath is on it, as they who fear you only know.

12.text: Which is by considering the shortness of our life, and by meditating the heavenly joys.

13.text: Meaning, will you be angry?

16.text: Even your mercy, which is the chiefest work.
As God’s promises belong well to their poverty, as to them, so Moses prays for the posterity.

17.text: Meaning, that is was obscured when he ceases to do good to his Church.
For unless you guide us with your Holy Spirit, our enterprises cannot succeed.

1.text: He who makes God his defence and trust will perceive his protection to be a most sure safeguard.

2.text: Being assured of this protection, he prays to the Lord.

3.text: That is, God’s help is most ready for us, whether Satan assails us secretly which he calls a snare, or openly which is here meant by the pestilence.

4.text: That is, his faithful keeping of promises to help you in your need.

5.text: The care that God has over his is sufficient to defend them from all dangers.

8.text: The godly will have some experience of God’s judgements against the wicked even in this life, but they will see it fully at that day when all things will be revealed.

11.text: God has not appointed one angel to every man, but many to be ministers of his providence to keep and defend his in their calling, which is the way to walk in without tempting God.

13.text: You will not only be preserved from all evil, but overcome it whether it is secret or open.

14.text: To assure the faithful of God’s protection, he brings in God to confirm the same.

16.text: For he is content with that life that God gives for by death the shortness of this life is recompensed with immortality.

1.text: Which teaches that the use of the Sabbath stands in praising God, and not only in ceasing from work.

2.text: For God’s mercy and fidelity in his promises toward his, bind them to praise him continually both day and night.

3.text: These instruments were then permitted in the Church as also they are now.

4.text: He shows the use of the Sabbath day: that is, to meditate God’s works.

6.text: That is, the wicked do not consider God’s works nor his judgments against them, and therefore most justly perish.

8.text: Your judgments are most constant against the wicked and pass our reach.

10.text: You will strengthen them with all power, and bless them with all happiness.

12.text: Though the faithful seem to whither and be cut down by the wicked, yet they will grow again and flourish in the Church of God as the cedars do in mount Lebanon.

14.text: The children of God will have a power above nature and their age will bring forth fresh fruit.

1.text: As God by his power and wisdom has made and governed the world, so must the same be our defence against all enemies and dangers.

2.text: In which you sit and govern the world.

3.text: God’s power appears in ruling the furious waters.

5.text: Besides God’s power and wisdom in creating and governing his great mercy also appears in that he has given his people his word and covenant.

1.text: Whose office it is to take vengeance on the wicked.
Show by effect that you are judge of the world to punish the wicked.

3.text: That is, brag of their cruelty and oppression, or esteem themselves above all others.

5.text: Seeing the Church was then so sore oppressed, it ought not to seem strange to us, if we see it so now, and therefore we must call to God, to take our cause in hand.

7.text: He shows that they are desperate in malice, as they did not fear God, but gave themselves wholly to do wickedly.

9.text: He shows that it is impossible, but God should hear, see, and understand their wickedness.

10.text: If God punishes whole nations for their sins, it is mere folly for any one man or else a few to think that God will spare them.

12.text: God has care over his, and chastised them for their own good, that they should not perish for ever with the wicked.

15.text: God will restore the state and government of things to their right use, and then the godly will follow him cheerfully.

17.text: He complains of them who would not help him to resist the enemies, yet was assured that God’s help would not fail.

18.text: When I thought there was no way but death.

19.text: In my trouble and distress I always found your present help.

20.text: Though the wicked judges pretend justice in oppressing the Church, yet they do not have the authority of God.

23.text: It is a great token of God’s judgment when the purpose of the wicked is broken, but most, when they are destroyed in their own malice.

1.text: He shows that God’s service stands not in dead ceremonies, but chiefly in the sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving.

3.text: Even the angels

4.text: All things are governed by his providence.

6.text: By these three words he signifies one thing: meaning that they must wholly give themselves to serve God.

7.text: That is, the flock whom he governs with his own hand. He shows how they are God’s flock, that is, if they hear his voice.

8.text: By the contemning of God’s word.

10.text: They were without judgment and reason.

11.text: That is, into the land of Canaan, where he promised them rest.

1.text: The prophet shows that the time will come, that all nations will have opportunity to praise the Lord for the revealing of his gospel.

4.text: Seeing he will reveal himself to all nations contrary to their own expectation, they should all worship him contrary to their own imaginations, and only as he has appointed.

5.text: Then the idols or whatever did not make the heavens, are not God.

6.text: God cannot be known but by his strength and glory, the signs of which appear in his sanctuary.

7.text: As by experience you see that it is only due to him.

8.text: By offering up yourselves wholly to God, declare that you worship him only.

10.text: He prophecies that the Gentiles will be partakers with the Jews of God’s promise.
He will regenerate them anew with his Spirit, and restore them to the image of God.

12.text: If the insensible creatures will have reason to rejoice when God appears, much more we, from whom he has taken malediction and sin.

1.text: He shows that where God reigns, there is all happiness and spiritual joy.
For the gospel will not only be preached in Judea, but through all isles and countries.

2.text: He is thus described to keep his enemies in fear, who commonly contemn God’s power.

4.text: This fear does not bring the wicked to true obedience, but makes them run away from God.

7.text: He signifies that God’s judgments are ready to destroy the idolatry.
Let all who are esteemed in the world fall down before him.

8.text: The Jews will have opportunity to rejoice that the Gentiles are made partakers with them of God’s favour.

10.text: He requires two things from his children: the one that they detest vice, the other, that they put their trust in God for their deliverance.

11.text: Though God’s deliverance does not appear suddenly, yet it is sown and laid up in store for them.

12.text: Be mindful of his benefits and only trust in his defence.

1.text: That is, some song newly made in token of their wonderful deliverance by Christ.
He preserves his Church miraculously.

2.text: For the deliverance of his Church.

3.text: God was moved by no other means to gather his Church from the Jews and Gentiles, but because he would perform his promise.

6.text: By this repetition and earnest exhortation to give praise with instruments, and also of the dumb creatures, he signifies that the world is never able to praise God sufficiently for their deliverance.

1.text: When God delivers his Church all the enemies will have reason to tremble.

3.text: Though the wicked rage against God, the godly will praise his Name and mighty power.

5.text: That is, before his temple or ark, where he promised to hear when they worshipped him, as now he promises his spiritual presence, wherever his Church is assembled.

6.text: Under these three he comprehends the whole people of Israel, with whom God made his promise.

8.text: The more liberally God deals with his people, the more he punishes them who abuse his benefits.

1.text: He prophecies that God’s benefits in calling the Gentiles will be so great that they will have wonderful opportunity to praise his mercy and rejoice.

3.text: He chiefly means concerning spiritual regeneration, by which we are his sheep and people.

4.text: He shows that God will not be worshipped, but by those means which he has appointed.

5.text: He declares that we should never be weary in praising him, seeing his mercies toward us last forever.

1.text: David considers what manner of King he would be, when God would place him in the throne, promising openly, that he would be merciful and just.

2.text: Though as yet you deferred to place me in the kingly dignity, yet I will give myself to wisdom and uprightness being a private man.

3.text: He shows that magistrates do not do their duties, unless they are enemies to all vice.

5.text: In promising to punish these vices, which are most pernicious in them that are about Kings, he declares that he will punish all.

6.text: He shows what the true use of the sword is, to punish the wicked and to maintain the good.

8.text: Magistrates must immediately punish vice, lest it grow to further inconvenience; and if heathen magistrates are bound to do this, how much more they who have the charge of the Church of God?

1.text: By which is signified, that even though we are in great misery, yet there is always room for prayer.
He declares that in our prayer we must lively feel that which we desire, and steadfastly believe to obtain.

3.text: These excessive kinds of speech show how much the affliction of the Church should wound the hearts of the godly.

4.text: My sorrows were so great that I did not eat.

6.text: Always mourning in solitude and casting out fearful cries.

8.text: Have conspired my death.

9.text: I have not risen out of my mourning to take my refreshment.

10.text: He shows that not only the afflictions moved him, but chiefly the feeling of God’s displeasure.

12.text: Though we are frail, yet your promise is sure, and the remembrance of it will confirm us forever.

13.text: That is, the seventy years which by the prophet Jeremiah you appointed, Jeremiah 29:12 .

14.text: The more the Church is in misery and desolation, the more the faithful should love and pity it.

16.text: That is, when he will have drawn his church out of the darkness of death.

18.text: The deliverance of the Church is an excellent benefit, and therefore he compares it to a new creation for in their banishment the body of the Church seemed to have been dead, which by deliverance was as it were created anew.

20.text: Who now in their banishment could look for nothing but death.

22.text: He shows that Gad’s name is never more praised, than when religion flourishes and the church increases: which is chiefly accomplished under the kingdom of Christ.

23.text: The church lament that they see not the time of Christ, which was promised, but have but few years and short days.

26.text: If heaven and earth perish, much more man will perish: but the Church by reason of God’s promise endures forever.

28.text: Seeing you have chosen your Church out of the world, and joined it to you, it cannot but continue forever: for you are everlasting.

1.text: He wakens his dulness to praise God, showing that both understanding and affections, mind and heart, are too little to set forth his praise.

3.text: That is, the beginning and chiefest of all benefits, remission of sin.

4.text: For before we have remission of our sins, we are as dead men in the grave.

5.text: As the eagle, when her beak overgrows, sucks blood and so is renewed in strength, even so God miraculously gives strength to his Church above all man’s expectations.

7.text: As to his chief minister, and next to his people.

9.text: He shows first his severe judgment, but as soon as the sinner is humbled, he receives him to mercy.

10.text: Who have proved by continual experience that his mercy has always prevailed against our offences.

12.text: As great as the world is, so full is it of signs of God’s mercies toward his faithful when he has removed their sins.

15.text: He declares that man has nothing in himself to move God to mercy, but only the confession of his infirmity and misery.

17.text: His just and faithful keeping of his promise.

18.text: To whom he gives grace to fear him, and to obey his word.

20.text: In that we, who naturally are slow to praise God, exhort the angels, who willingly do it, we stir up ourselves to consider our duty and wake from our sluggishness.

1.text: The prophet shows that we do not need to enter into the heavens to seek God, for as much as all the order of nature, with the propriety and placing of the elements, are living mirrors to see his majesty in.

4.text: As the prophet here shows that all visible powers are ready to serve God: so in Hebrews 1:7 the angels also, are obedient to his commandment.

6.text: You make the sea to be an ornament to the earth.
If by your power you did not bridle the rage of the waters, the whole world would be destroyed.

11.text: If God provides for the beasts, much more will he extend his provident care to man.

12.text: There is no part of the world so barren where most evident signs of God’s blessing do not appear.

13.text: From the clouds.

14.text: He describes God’s providential care over man, who not only provides necessary things for him such as herbs and other meat: but also things to rejoice and comfort him such as wine and oil or ointments.

19.text: As to separate the night from the day, and to note days, months and years.
That is, by his course, either far or near, it notes summer, winter and other seasons.

23.text: That is, when the day springs for the light is as it were a shield to defend man against the tyranny and fierceness of beasts.

24.text: He confesses that no tongue is able to express God’s works nor mind to comprehend them.

27.text: God is a nourishing father, who provides for all creatures their daily foods.

29.text: As by your presence all things have life; so if you withdraw your blessings they all perish.

30.text: As the death of creatures shows that we are nothing of ourselves: so their generation declares that we receive all things from our Creator.

32.text: God’s merciful face gives strength to the earth, but his severe countenance burns the mountains.

35.text: Who infect the world, and so cause it to be that God cannot rejoice in his work.

1.text: For as much as the Israelites were exempted from the common condemnation of the world, and were elected to be God’s people, the prophet wills them to show themselves mindful by thanksgiving.

4.text: By the strength and face he means the ark where God declared his power and his presence.

5.text: Which he has wrought in the deliverance of his people.
Because his power was declared living by this, as if he would have declared it by mouth.

9.text: The promise God made to Abraham to be his God, and the God of his seed after him, he renewed and repeated again to his seed after him.

11.text: He shows that they would not enjoy the land of Canaan by any other means, but by reason of his covenant made with their fathers.

14.text: That is, the king of Egypt and the king of Gerar, Genesis 12:17 ; Genesis 20:3

15.text: Those whom I have sanctified to be my people.
Meaning, the old fathers, to whom God showed himself plainly, and who set forth his word.

16.text: Either by sending scarcity or the strength and nourishment of it.

19.text: So long he suffered adversity as God had appointed, and till he had sufficiently tried his patience.

22.text: That the very princes of the countries would be at Joseph’s commandment, and learn wisdom from him.

25.text: So it is in God, either to move the hearts of the wicked to love or to hate God’s children.

28.text: Meaning, Moses and Aaron.

31.text: So that this vermin did not come by chance, but as God had appointed, and his prophet Moses spoke.

32.text: It was strange to see rain in Egypt, much more it was fearful to see hail.

34.text: He shows that all creatures are armed against man when God is his enemy as at his commandment the grasshoppers destroyed the land.

37.text: When their enemies felt God’s plagues his children by his providence were exempted.

38.text: For God’s plagues caused them to prefer to depart with the Israelites rather than with their lives.

40.text: Not for necessity but for satisfying of their lust.

42.text: Which he confirms to the posterity in whom after a sort the dead live and enjoy the promises.

43.text: When the Egyptians lamented and were destroyed.

45.text: This is the reason why God preserves his Church, because they should worship and call on him in this world.

1.text: The prophet exhorts the people to praise God for his past benefits, that by this their minds may be strengthened against all present troubles and despair.

3.text: He shows that it is not enough to praise God with the mouth, unless the whole heart agrees to it, and all our life framed after it.

4.text: Let the good will that you bear to your people extend to me, that by it I may be received into your number.

6.text: By earnest confession of their sins and of their father’s, they show that they hoped that God according to his promise would pity them.

8.text: The inestimable goodness of God appears in this, that he would rather change the order of nature than have his people not be delivered, even though they were wicked.

12.text: The wonderful words of God caused them to believe for a time, and to praise him.

13.text: The would prevent his wisdom and providence.

15.text: The abundance that God gave them did not profit, but made them pine away, because God cursed it.

17.text: By the greatness of the punishment the heinousness of the offence may be considered: for they who rise against God’s ministers rebel against him.

20.text: He shows that all idolaters renounce God to be their glory when instead of him, they worship any creature much more wood, stone, metal or calves.

23.text: If Moses, by his intercession, had not obtained God’s favour against their rebellion.

24.text: That is Canaan, which acted as a promise of the heavenly inheritance to come, though it was only worth a penny in comparison to the value of the inheritance itself.

26.text: That is, he swore. Sometimes also it means to punish.

28.text: Which was the idol of the Moabites.
Sacrifices offered to the dead idols.

29.text: Signifying that whatever man invents of himself to serve God by, is detestable and provokes his anger.

30.text: When all others neglected God’s glory, he in his zeal killed the adulterers and prevented God’s wrath.

31.text: This act declared his living faith, and for his faith’s sake was accepted.

32.text: If so notable a prophet of God does not escape punishment, though others provoked him to sin, how much more will they be subject to God’s judgment, who cause God’s children to sin?

37.text: He shows how monstrous a thing idolatry is, which can win us to things abhorring to nature, while God’s word cannot obtain small things.

39.text: Then true chastity is to cleave wholly and only to God.

43.text: The prophet shows that neither by menace nor promise we can come to God, unless we are altogether newly reformed, and his mercy covers and hides our malice.

45.text: Not that God is changeable in himself, but that then he seems to us to repent when he alters his punishment, and forgives us.

47.text: Gather your Church which is dispersed, and give us constancy under the cross, that with one consent we may all praise you.

1.text: This notable sentence was in the beginning used as the foot or tenor of the song, which was often repeated.

2.text: As was true in the Jews, so there is not one of God’s elect who does not feel his help in their necessity.

5.text: He shows that there is no affliction so grievous out of which God will not deliver us, and also exhorts them who are delivered to be mindful of so great a benefit.

11.text: Then the true way to obey God is to follow his express commandment: also by this all are exhorted to descend into themselves as none are punished but for their sins.

13.text: He shows that the reason God punishes us extremely is because we can be brought to him by no other means.

16.text: When there seems to man’s judgment no recovery, but all things are brought to despair, then God chiefly shows his mighty power.

17.text: They who have no fear of God, by his sharp rods are brought to call on him, and so find mercy.

20.text: By healing them he declares his good will toward them.
Meaning their diseases, which had almost brought them to the grave and corruption.

22.text: Praise and confession of God’s benefits are the true sacrifices of the godly.

23.text: He shows by the sea what care God has over man, for when he delivers them from the great danger of the sea, he delivers them as it were from a thousand deaths.

26.text: Their fear and danger is so great.

27.text: When their art and means fail them, they are compelled to confess that only God’s providence preserves them.

1.text: He comforts the Church again after these great threatenings promising to restore them to great glory in Messiah.
With which Israel was punished, first by Tiglath-pilesar, which was a light scourge in respect to that which they suffered afterward by Shalmaneser, who carried the Israelites away captive.
While the Jews and Gentiles dwelt together by reason of those twenty cites, which Solomon gave to Hiram.

2.text: Which were in captivity in Babylon and the prophets speaks of that thing which would come to pass 60 years later as though it were now done.
Meaning, the comfort of their deliverance.
This captivity and deliverance were figures of our captivity by sin and of our deliverance by Christ through the preaching of the Gospel, Matthew 4:15-16 .

3.text: Their number was greater when they went into captivity then when they returned but their joy was greater at their return, Haggai 2:9 .

4.text: You gave them perfect joy by delivering them, and by destroying the tyrants, that had kept them in cruel bondage, as you delivered them by Gideon from the Midianites, Jud 7:21 .

5.text: He speaks of the deliverance of his Church, which he has delivered miraculously from his enemies, but especially by the coming of Christ of whom he prophecies in the next verse.

6.text: The author of eternity, and by whom the Church and every member of it will be preserved forever, and have immortal life.

7.text: His singular love and care for his elect.

8.text: This is another prophecy against them of Samaria who were mockers and contemners of God’s promises and menaces.

10.text: We were but weak, when the enemy overcame us, but we will make ourselves so strong, that we will neither care for our enemies, nor fear God’s threatenings.

11.text: Rezin king of Syria, who was in league with Israel, was slain by the Assyrians, after whose death, Aram that is, the Syrians were against Israel, who on the other side were assailed by the Philistines.

18.text: Wickedness as a bellows kindles the fire of God’s wrath which consumes all his obstinate enemies.

19.text: Though there was no foreign enemy, yet they will destroy one another.

20.text: Their greediness will be insatiable, so that one brother will eat up another, as though he should eat his own flesh.

1.text: Who write and pronounce a wicked sentence to oppress the people: meaning, that the wicked magistrate, who were the chief cause of mischief, would be first punished.

3.text: That is, from Assyria.
Your riches and authority, that they may be safe and that you may receive them again.

4.text: Because they have forsaken me, some will go into captivity and the rest will be slain.

5.text: God calls for the Assyrians to be the executioners of his vengeance.

6.text: That is, the Assyrians against the Jews who are hypocrites. In the sixth and seventh verse is declared the difference of the work of God and of the wicked in one very thing and act: for God’s intention is to chastise them for their amendment, and the Assyrians purpose is to destroy them to enrich themselves. Thus in respect to God’s justice, it is God’s work, but in respect to their own malice, it is the work of the devil.

9.text: Seeing that I have overcome one city as well as another, so that none could resist, shall Jerusalem be able to escape my hands?

12.text: When he has sufficiently chastised his people (for he begins at his own house) then will he burn the rods.
Meaning of Sennacherib.

15.text: Here we see that no creature is able to do anything, but as God appoints him, and that they are all his instruments to do his work though the intentions are diverse, as in Isaiah 10:6 .

17.text: Meaning that God is a light to comfort his people and a fire to burn his enemies.
That is, the Assyrians.

18.text: That is, body and soul utterly.
When the battle is lost and the standard taken.

20.text: This is the end of God’s plagues toward his, to bring them to him, and to forsake all trust in others.

22.text: This small number which seemed to be consumed and yet according to God’s decree is saved, will be sufficient to fill all the world with righteousness.

23.text: God will destroy this land as he has determined and later save a small portion.

24.text: As the Egyptians punished you.

26.text: Read Isaiah 9:4 .
When the Israelites passed through by the lifting up of Moses’ rod, and the enemies were drowned, Exodus 14:28 .

27.text: Because of the promise made to that kingdom, by which Christ’s kingdom was prefigured.

28.text: He describes by what way the Assyrians would come against Jerusalem, to confirm the faithful, when it would come to pass, that as their plague was come, so should they be delivered.

33.text: Fear and destruction will come on Judah for the princes and the people will all be led away captive.

1.text: Because the captivity of Babylon was a figure of the spiritual captivity under sin, he shows that our true deliverance must come by Christ: for as David came out of Jesse, a man without dignity, so Christ would come of a poor carpenter’s house as out of a dead stock, Isaiah 53:2 .

4.text: All these properties can agree to no one, but only to Christ: for it is he who touches the hearts of the faithful and mortifies their concupiscence: and to the wicked he is the favour of death and to them who will perish, so that all the world will be smitten with his rod, which is his word.

6.text: Men because of their wicked affections are named by the names of beasts, in which the same affections reign: but Christ by his Spirit will reform them, and work in them such mutual charity, that they will be like lambs, favouring and loving one another and cast off all their cruel affections, Isaiah 65:25 .

9.text: It will be in as great abundance as the waters in the sea.

10.text: He prophecies of the calling of the Gentiles.
That is, the Church which he also calls his rest, Psalms 132:14 .

11.text: For God first delivered his people out of Egypt and now promises to deliver them out of their enemies hands as from the Parthians, Persians, Chaldeans and them of Antioch among whom they were dispersed and this is chiefly meant of Christ, who calls his people being dispersed through all the world.

13.text: Here he describes the consent that will be in his Church and their victory against their enemies.

15.text: Meaning a corner of the sea that enters into the land and has the form of a tongue.
That is, Nile, the great river of Egypt which enters into the sea with seven streams.

1.text: He shows how the Church will praise God, when they are delivered from their captivity.

2.text: Our salvation stands only in God, who gives us an assured confidence, constancy and opportunity to praise him for the same.

3.text: The graces of God will be so abundant that you may receive them in as great plenty as waters out of a fountain that is full.

6.text: You who are of the Church.

1.text: That is, the great calamity which was prophesied to come on Babel, a grievous burden which they were not able to bear. In these twelve chapters following he speaks of the plagues with which God would smite the strange nations (whom they knew) to declare that God chastised the Israelites as his children and these others as his enemies: and also that if God does not spare these who are ignorant, they must not think strange if he punishes them who have knowledge of his Law, and do not keep it.

2.text: That is, the Medes and Persians.

3.text: That is, prepared and appointed to execute my judgments.
Who willingly go about to the work to which I appoint them, but how the wicked do this, read Isaiah 10:6 .

5.text: The army of the Medes and the Persians against Babylon.

6.text: You Babylonians.

8.text: The Babylonians anger and grief will be so much that their faces will burn as fire.

10.text: They who are overcome will think that all the powers of heaven and earth are against them, Ezekiel 32:7 , Joel 3:15 , Matthew 24:29 .

11.text: He compares Babylon to the whole world because they so esteemed themselves by reason of their great empire.
He notes the principal vice, to which they are most given as are all that abound in wealth.

12.text: He notes the great slaughter that will be, seeing the enemy will neither for gold or silver spare a man’s life as in Isaiah 13:17 .

14.text: Meaning the power of Babylon with their hired soldiers.

16.text: This was not accomplished when Cyrus took Babylon, but after the death of Alexander the great.

20.text: Who used to go from country to country to find pasture for their beasts, but they will find none.

21.text: Who were either wild beasts or fools, or wicked spirits, by which Satan deluded man, as by the fairies, goblins, and such like fantasies.

1.text: He shows why God will haste to destroy his enemies, that is, because he will deliver his Church.
Meaning that the Gentiles will be joined with the Church and worship God.

2.text: Signifying that the Jews would be superior to the Gentiles and that they would be brought under the service of Christ by the preaching of the Apostles, by which all are brought to the subjection of Christ, 2 Corinthians 10:5 .

6.text: That is, he permitted all violence and injuries to be done.

7.text: Meaning that where tyrants reign, there can be no rest or quietness and also how detestable a thing tyranny is, seeing the insensible creatures have opportunity to rejoice at their destruction.

9.text: As though they feared, lest you should trouble the dead, as you did the living and here he derides the proud tyranny of the wicked, who know not that all creatures wish their destruction, that they may rejoice.

11.text: Instead of your costly carpets and coverings.

12.text: You who thought yourself most glorious and as it were placed in the heaven for the morning star that goes before the sun, is called Lucifer, to whom Nebuchadnezzar is compared.

13.text: Meaning, Jerusalem of which the temple was of the north side, Psalms 48:2 .

16.text: In marvelling at you.

17.text: To set them free, noting his cruelty.

19.text: You were not buried in the sepulchre of your fathers, your tyranny was so abhorred.

21.text: He called to the Medes and Persians, and all those who would execute God’s vengeance.

25.text: As I have begun to destroy the Assyrians in Sennacherib: so will I continue and destroy them wholly, when I will deliver you from Babylon.
From the Jews.

28.text: Read Geneva " Isaiah 13:1 "

29.text: He wills the Philistines not to rejoice because the Jews are diminished in their power, for their strength will be greater than it ever was.

30.text: The Israelites who were brought to most extreme misery.
That is, my people.

31.text: That is, from the Jews or Assyrians: for they were brought to extreme misery.

32.text: Who will come to enquire of the state of the Church.
They will answer that the Lord defends his Church and those that join themselves to it.

1.text: Read Geneva " Isaiah 13:1 "
The chief city by which the whole country was meant.

2.text: The Moabites will flee to their idols for comfort but it will be too late.
Which were cites of Moab.
For as in the west parts the people used to let their hair grow long when they mourned, so in the East part they cut it off.

5.text: The prophet speaks this in the person of the Moabites: or as one who felt the great judgment of God that God would come on them.
Meaning that it was a city that always lived in pleasure and never felt sorrow.
He describes the miserable dissipation and flight of the Moabites.

7.text: To hide themselves and their goods there.

9.text: Of them who are slain.
So that by no means would they escape the hand of God: thus will God punish the enemies of his Church.

1.text: That is, offer a sacrifice, by which he derides their long delay, who would not repent when the Lord called them, showing them that it is now too late seeing the vengeance of God is on them.

2.text: There is no remedy but that you must flee.

3.text: He shows what Moab would have done, when Israel their neighbour was in affliction, to whom because they would give no shadow or comfort, they are now left comfortless.

4.text: The Assyrians will oppress the Israelites but for a while.

5.text: Meaning, Christ.

6.text: Their vain confidence and proud bragging will deceive them, Jeremiah 48:2 .

7.text: For all your mourning, yet the city will be destroyed even to the foundation.

8.text: That is, the Assyrians and other enemies.
Meaning that the country of Moab was now destroyed, and all the precious things of it were carried into the borders yea into other countries and over the sea.

9.text: He shows that their plague was so great that it would have moved any man to lament with them, as in Psalms 141:5 .
The enemies are come upon you, and shout for joy when they carry your conveniences from you as in Jeremiah 48:33 .

11.text: For sorrow and compassion.

12.text: They will use all means to seek help for their idols, and all in vain: for Chemosh their great god will not be able to help them.

14.text: He appointed a certain time to punish the enemies in.
Who will observe justly the time for which he is hired and serve no longer but will ever long for it.

1.text: Read Geneva " Isaiah 13:1 "
The chief city of Syria.

2.text: It was a country of Syria by the river Arnon.

3.text: It seems that the prophet would comfort the Church in declaring the destruction of these two kings of Syria and Israel, when as they had conspired the overthrow of Judah.
The ten tribes gloried in their multitude and alliance with other nations: therefore he says that they will be brought down and the Syrians also.

4.text: Meaning, of the ten tribes who boasted themselves of their nobility, prosperity, strength and multitude.

5.text: As the abundance of corn does not fear the harvest men that would cut it down: no more will the multitude of Israel make the enemies shrink, whom God will appoint to destroy them.
A valley which was plentiful and fertile.

6.text: Because God would have his covenant stable, he promises to reserve some of this people, and to bring them to repentance.

7.text: He shows that God’s corrections always bring fruit, and cause his to turn from their sins and to humble themselves to him.

9.text: As the Canaanites left their cities when God placed the Israelites there, so the cities of Israel will not be able to defend their inhabitants any more than bushes, when God will send the enemy to plague them.

10.text: Which are excellent and brought out of other countries.

11.text: As the Lord threatens the wicked in his law, Leviticus 26:16 .

12.text: The prophet laments, considering the horrible plague that was prepared against Israel by the Assyrians, who were infinite in number, and gathered from many nations.

13.text: He adds this for the consolation of the faithful who were in Israel.

14.text: He compares the Assyrians to a tempest which rises overnight and in the morning is gone.

1.text: He means that part of Ethiopia which lies toward the sea, which was so full of ships that the sails (which he compares to wings) seemed to shadow the sea.

2.text: Which is those countries were great, so much so that they made ships from them for swiftness.

This may be taken that they sent others to comfort the Jews and to promise them help against their enemies, and so the Lord threatened to take away their strength, that the Jews should not trust in it: or that they solicited the Egyptians and promised them aid to go against Judah.
That is, the Jews who because of God’s plague made all other nations afraid of the same, as God threatened in De 28:37 .
Meaning the Assyrians, Isaiah 8:7 .

3.text: When the Lord prepared to fight against the Ethiopians.

4.text: I will stay a while from punishing the wicked.
Which two seasons are profitable for the ripening of fruit, by which he means that he will seem to favour them and give them abundance for a time, but he will suddenly cut them off.

6.text: Not only men will contemn them, but the brute beast.

7.text: Meaning that God will pity his Church, and receive that little remnant as an offering to himself.

1.text: Read Isaiah 13:7 .

Because the Egyptians trusted in the defence of their country, in the multitude of their idols and in the valiantness of their men the Lord shows that he will come over all their munitions in a swift cloud, and that their idols will tremble at his coming and that men’s hearts will faint.

2.text: As he caused the Ammonites, Moabites and Idumeans to kill one another, when they came to destroy the Church of God, 2 Chronicles 20:22 , Isaiah 49:26 .

3.text: Meaning, their policy and wisdom.

5.text: He shows that the sea and their great river Nile by which they thought themselves most sure, would not be able to defend them but that he would send the Assyrians among them, that would keep them under as slaves.

6.text: For the Nile ran into the sea by seven streams, as though they were many rivers.

7.text: The Hebrew word is mouth, by which they mean the spring out of which the water gushes as out of a mouth.

8.text: The Scriptures describe the destruction of a country by the taking away of the conveniences of it, as by vines, flesh, fish and such other things by which countries are enriched.

11.text: Called also Tanes, a famous city on the Nile.
He notes the flatterers of Pharaoh: who persuaded the king that he was wise and noble, and that his house was ancient and so he flatters himself, saying I am wise.

13.text: Or Memphis, Alexandria, and now called the great Cairo.
The principal upholders of it are the main cause of their destruction.

14.text: For the spirit of wisdom he has made them drunken and giddy with the spirit of error.

15.text: Neither the great or the small, the strong or the weak.

17.text: Considering that through their opportunity the Jews did not make God their defence but put their trust in them, and were therefore now punished, they will fear least the same light on them.

18.text: Will make one confession of faith with the people of God, by the speech of Canaan, meaning the language in which God was then served.
Will renounce their superstitions and protest to serve God correctly.
Meaning of six cities, five would serve God, and the sixth would remain in their wickedness: and so there would be but one lost.

19.text: There will be evident signs and tokens, that God’s religion is there: which manner of speech is taken of the patriarchs and ancient time, when God has not as yet appointed the place, and full manner how he would be worshipped.

20.text: This declares that this prophecy would be accomplished in the time of Christ.

21.text: By these ceremonies he comprehends the spiritual service under Christ.

23.text: By these two nations, which were then chief enemies of the Church, he shows that the Gentiles and the Jews would be joined together in one faith and religion, and would all be one fold under Christ their shepherd.

1.text: Who was captain of Sennacherib, 2 Kings 18:17 .
A city of the Philistines.
The Hebrews write that Sennacherib was so called.

2.text: Which signifies that the prophet lamented the misery that he saw prepared before the three years that he went naked and barefooted.

5.text: In whose aid they trusted.
Of whom they boasted and gloried.

6.text: Meaning Judea which was encompassed by their enemies as an isle with waters.

1.text: On the seaside between Judea and Caldea was a wilderness, by which he means Caldea.
That is, the ruin of Babylon by the Medes and Persians.

2.text: The Assyrians and Chaldeans who had destroyed other nations will be overcome by the Medes and Persians: and this he prophesied a hundred years before it came to pass.
By Elam he means the Persians.
Because they will find no comfort, they will mourn no more, or I have caused them to cease mourning, whom Babylon had afflicted.

3.text: This the prophet speaks in the person of the Babylonians.

4.text: He prophecies the death of Belshazzar as in Daniel 5:30 who in the midst of his pleasures was destroyed.

5.text: While they are eating and drinking, they will be commanded to run to their weapons.

6.text: That is, in a vision by the spirit of prophecy.

7.text: Meaning, chariots of men of war, and others that carried the baggage.

8.text: Meaning, Darius who overcame Babylon.

9.text: The watchman whom Isaiah set up, told him who came toward Babylon, and the angel declared that it would be destroyed: all this was done in a vision.

10.text: Meaning, Babylon.

11.text: Which was a city of the Ishmaelites and was so named by Dumah, Genesis 25:14 .
A mountain of the Idumeans.

12.text: He describes the unquietness of the people of Dumah, who were night and day in fear of their enemies, and ever ran to and fro to enquire news.

13.text: For fear, the Arabians will flee into the woods and he appoints the way they will take.

14.text: Signifying that for fear they will not tarry to eat or drink.

16.text: He appoints them respite for one year only, and then they would be destroyed.
Read Isaiah 16:14 .

17.text: Which was the name of a people of Arabia: and by the horrible destruction of all these nations, he teaches the Jews that there is no place for refuge or to escape God’s wrath, but only to remain in his Church, and to live in his fear.

1.text: Meaning, Judea, which was compassed about with mountains, and was called the valley of visions, because of the prophets, who were always there, whom they named Seers.
He speaks to Jerusalem, whose inhabitants fled up to the housetops for fear of their enemies.

2.text: Which was wont to be full of people and joy.
But for hunger.

3.text: And led into captivity.
Who have fled from other places to Jerusalem for comfort.

4.text: He shows what is the duty of the godly, when God’s plagues hang over the Church, and especially of the ministers, Jeremiah 9:1 .

5.text: That is, the shout of the enemies whom God had appointed to destroy the city.

6.text: He reminds them how God delivered them once from Sennacherib, who brought the Persians and Syrians with him, that they might by returning to God avoid that great plague which they would suffer by Nebuchadnezzar.

8.text: The secret place where the armour was: that is, in the house of the forest, 1 Kings 7:2 .

9.text: You forfeited the ruinous places which were neglected in times of peace: meaning, the whole City, and the City of David, which was within the compass of the other.

10.text: Either to pull down such as might hurt, or else to know what men they were able to make.

11.text: To provide if need should be of water.
To God who made Jerusalem: that is, they trusted more in these worldly means than in God.

13.text: Instead of repentance you were joyful and made great cheer, contemning the admonitions of the prophets saying Let us eat and drink for our prophets say that we will die tomorrow.

15.text: Because the Hebrew word also signifies one who nourishes and cherishes, there are those of the scholars who think that this wicked man nourished a secret friendship with the Assyrians and Egyptians to betray the Church and to provide for himself against all dangers: in the mean season he packed craftily, and got of the best offices into his hand under Hezekiah, ever aspiring to the highest.

16.text: Meaning, that he was a stranger, and came up of nothing.
While he thought to make his name immortal by his famous sepulchre, he died most miserably among the Assyrians.

18.text: Signifying that whatever dignity the wicked attain to, at length it will turn to the shame of those princes by whom they are preferred.

20.text: To be steward again, out of which office he had been put, by the craft of Shebna.

22.text: I will commit to him the full charge and government of the king’s house.

23.text: I will establish him, and confirm him in his office, of this phrase read Ezra 9:9 .

24.text: Meaning that both small and great who will come from Eliakim, will have praise and glory by his faithful officer.

25.text: He means Shebna, who in man’s judgment should never have fallen.

1.text: Read Geneva " Isaiah 13:1 "
You of Cilicia that come here for merchandise.
Tyrus is destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar.
By Chittim they meant all the isles and countries west of Palestine.
All men know of this destruction.

2.text: Have hunted and enriched you.

3.text: Meaning, the corn of Egypt which was fed by the overflowing of the Nile.

4.text: That is, Tyrus, which was the chief part of the sea.
I have no people left in me, and am as a barren woman, that never had children.

5.text: Because these two countries were joined in league together.

6.text: Tyrus wills other merchants to go to Cilicia, and to come no more there.

8.text: Who makes her merchants like princes.

10.text: Your strength will no more serve you: therefore flee to other countries for comfort.

12.text: For Tyre was never touched nor afflicted before.
Because Tyrus was built by them of Zidon.

13.text: The Chaldeans who dwelt in tents in the wilderness were gathered by the Assyrians into cities.

The people of the Chaldeans destroyed the Assyrians: by which the prophet means that seeing the Chaldaeans were able to overcome the Assyrians who were so great a nation, much more will these two nations of Chaldea and Assyria be able to overthrow Tyrus.

14.text: That is, Tyrus by whom you are enriched.

15.text: Tyrus will lie destroyed seventy years which he calls the reign of one king, or a man’s age.
Will use all craft and subtilty to entice men again to her.

16.text: She will labour by all means to recover her first credit, as a harlot when she is long forgotten, seeks by all means to entertain her lovers.

17.text: Though she has been chastised by the Lord, yet she will return to her old wicked practises and for gain will give herself to all men’s lusts like a harlot.

18.text: He shows that God yet by the preaching of the gospel will call Tyre to repentance and turn her heart from evil and filthy gain, to the true worshipping of God, and liberality toward his saints.

1.text: This prophecy is as a conclusion of that which has been threatened to the Jews and other nations from the 13th chapter and therefore by the earth he means those lands which were named before.

2.text: Because this was a name of dignity it was also applied to them who were not of Aaron’s family, and so signifies also a man of dignity, as in 2 Samuel 8:18 ; 2 Samuel 20:25 , 1 Chronicles 18:17 and by these words the prophet signifies a horrible confusion, where there will be neither religion, order nor policy, Hosea 4:9 .

5.text: That is, does not give her fruit for the sin of the people, whom the earth deceived of their nourishment because they deceived God of his honour.

6.text: Written in the law, as in Leviticus 26:14 , De 28:16 thus the prophets used to apply particularly the menaces and promises which are general in the law.
With heat and drought, or else that they were consumed with the fire of God’s wrath.

10.text: Which as it was without order so now should it be brought to desolation and confusion: and this was not only meant of Jerusalem, but of all the other wicked cities.

11.text: Because they did not use God’s benefits correctly their pleasures would fail, and they would fall to mourning.

13.text: He comforts the faithful, declaring that in this great desolation the Lord will assemble his Church which will praise his Name, as in Isaiah 10:22 .

14.text: From the utmost coasts of the world, where the gospel will be preached as in Isaiah 24:16 .

16.text: Meaning to God, who will publish his gospel through all the world.

I am consumed with care, considering the affliction of the Church, both by foreign enemies and domestic. Some read, My secret, my secret: that is, it was revealed to the prophet, that the good would be preserved and the wicked destroyed.

18.text: Meaning that God’s wrath and vengeance would be over and under them, so that they would not escape no more than they did at Noah’s flood.

21.text: There is no power so high or mighty, but God will visit him with his rods.

22.text: Not with his rods as in Isaiah 24:21 but will be comforted.

23.text: When God restores his Church, the glory of it will so shine, and his ministers (who are called his ancient men) that the sun and the moon will be dark in comparison to it.

1.text: Thus the prophet gives thanks to God because he will bring under subjection these nations by his corrections, and make them of his Church, who before were his enemies.

2.text: Not only of Jerusalem, but also of these other cities which have been your enemies.
That is, a place where all vagabonds may live without danger and as it were at ease as in a palace.

3.text: The arrogant and proud who before would not know you will by your corrections fear and glorify you.

4.text: The rage of the wicked is furious, till God breaks the force of it.

5.text: Meaning, that as the heat is abated by the rain, so shall God bring down the rage of the wicked.
As a cloud shades from the heat of the sun, so God will assuage the rejoicing of the wicked against the godly.

6.text: That is, in Zion, by which he means his Church, which would under Christ be assembled of the Jews and the Gentiles, and is here described under the figure of a costly banquet, as in Matthew 22:2 .

7.text: Meaning, that ignorance and blindness, by which we are kept back from Christ.

8.text: He will take away all opportunity for sorrow and fill his with perfect joy, Revelation 7:17 ; Revelation 21:4 .

10.text: By Moab are meant all the enemies of his Church.
There were two cities by this name: one in Judah, 1 Chronicles 6:81 and another in the land of Moab, Jeremiah 48:2 which seems to have been a plentiful place of corn, Isaiah 36:17 .

1.text: This song was made to comfort the faithful when their captivity would come, assuring them also of their deliverance, for which they should sing this song.
God’s protection and defence will be sufficient for us.

2.text: He assures the godly to return after the captivity to Jerusalem.

3.text: You have decreed so, and your purpose cannot be changed.

5.text: There is no power so high that it can hinder God, when he will deliver his.

6.text: God will set the poor afflicted over the power of the wicked.

8.text: We have constantly abode in the adversities with which you had afflicted us.

9.text: Meaning that by afflictions men will learn to fear God.

10.text: The wicked though God show them evident signs of his grace, will not be any better off.

11.text: Through envy and indignation against your people.
The fire and vengeance with which you destroy your enemies.

13.text: The Babylonians, who have not governed according to your word.

14.text: Meaning that the reprobate even in this life will have the beginning of everlasting death.

15.text: That is, the company of the faithful by the calling of the Gentiles.

16.text: That is, the faithful by the rods were moved to pray to you for deliverance.

17.text: That is, in extreme sorrow.

18.text: Our sorrows had no end, neither did we enjoy the comfort that we looked for.
The wicked and men without religion were not destroyed.

19.text: He comforts the faithful in their afflictions, showing them that even in death they will have life and that they would certainly rise to glory, the contrary would come to the wicked, as in Isaiah 26:14 .
As herbs dead in winter flourish again by the rain in the springtime, so they who lie in the dust will rise up to joy, when they feel the dew of God’s grace.

20.text: He exhorts the faithful to be patient in their afflictions and to wait on God’s work.

21.text: The earth will vomit and cast out the innocent blood, which it has drunk, that it may care for vengeance against the wicked.

1.text: At the time appointed.
That is, by his mighty power, and by his word. He prophecies here of the destruction of Satan and his kingdom under the name of Liviashan, Assur, and Egypt.

2.text: Meaning, of the best wine, which this vineyard, that is, the Church would bring forth, as most agreeable to the Lord.

4.text: Therefore he will destroy the kingdom of Satan, because he loves his Church for his own mercies sake, and cannot be angry with it, but wishes that he may pour his anger on the wicked infidels, whom he means by briers and thorns.

5.text: He marvels that Israel will not come by gentleness, unless God make them to feel his rods, and so bring them to him.

6.text: Though I afflict and diminish my people for a time, yet will the root spring again and bring forth in great abundance.

7.text: He shows that God punishes his in mercy, and his enemies in justice.

8.text: That is, you will not destroy the root of your Church, though the branches of it seem to perish by the sharp wind of affliction.

9.text: He shows that there is no true repentance nor full reconciliation to God, till the heart is purged from all idolatry and the monuments of it are destroyed.

10.text: Not withstanding his favour that he will show them later, yet Jerusalem will be destroyed, and grass for cattle will grow in it.

11.text: God will not have need of mighty enemies: for the very women will do it to their great shame.

12.text: He will destroy all from the Euphrates to the Nile: for some fled toward Egypt, thinking to have escaped.

13.text: In the time of Cyrus, by whom they would be delivered: but this was chiefly accomplished under Christ.

1.text: Meaning, the proud kingdom of the Israelites, who were drunk with worldly prosperity.
Because the Israelites for the most part dwelt in plentiful valleys, he means by this the valley of them who had abundance of worldly prosperity and were as it were crowned with garlands.

2.text: He seems to mean the Assyrians, by whom the ten tribes were carried away.

4.text: Which is not of long continuance, but is soon ripe and first eaten.

5.text: Signifying that the faithful who do not put their trust in any worldly prosperity but made God their glory, will be preserved.

6.text: He will give counsel to the governor and strength to the captain to drive the enemies in at their own gates.

7.text: Meaning, the hypocrites who were among them, and were altogether corrupt in life and doctrine, which is here meant by drunkenness and vomiting.
